historical_record.description: The Union Oil Company Building, designed in 1940 by Lewis P. Hobart and built in 1940–41 by MacDonald & Kahn, stood here: three storeys and a penthouse in steel frame and reinforced concrete, faced in terra cotta, roman brick and glass block. It was one of a handful of transitional Streamline Moderne and International Style office buildings in the city, and among the few major corporate offices of its day built outside the Financial District.

The Union Oil Company Building, a Streamline Moderne office building whose non-functional tower carried neon signage visible from the 1939 Golden Gate International Exposition; expanded in the early 1950s and later demolished for a high-rise luxury condominium project.

The Union Oil Company Building was enlarged in 1953–55 to designs by Ralph N. Kerr, which replaced the rectangular clock tower with a triangular one 183 feet tall, facing traffic off the Bay Bridge. A parking structure along the north wall followed in 1955, and the tower and interior were altered again in 1995.
The Union Oil Company Building, designed by Lewis P. Hobart, was demolished to make way for the present tower.
A former Bank of America three-story office building, clock tower, and two-story parking garage stood at the property.
The City Planning Commission certified the Final Environmental Impact Report for the One Rincon Hill residential development at 425 First Street.
The City Planning Commission adopted the California Environmental Quality Act findings for the One Rincon Hill residential development at 425 First Street.
The City Planning Commission approved the determinations of compliance under Planning Code Section 309.1 for the One Rincon Hill residential project at 425 First Street.
The City Planning Commission approved the Mello-Roos Agreement to satisfy the Rincon Hill Community Infrastructure Impact Fee requirement for the project at 425 First Street.
